Action items assigned for logs, canonical prompts, and runbook updates.

Next benchmark run and metrics to capture
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-03-12 15:00 PT | Duration: ~42m | Attendees: Lena Ortega, Marcus Chen, Priya Patel (Redwood); Rachel Kim, Tom Alvarez, Priya Singh (Novus)

00:00 Lena Ortega: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — hit-rate review, prompt reuse approach, and next steps for the pilot. Marcus, do you want to kick us off with the telemetry?
00:28 Marcus Chen: Yeah sure. I'll share screen in a sec. So we ingested the last 72 hours of traffic and ran grouping by prompt fingerprint. High level — overall KV/prefix cache hit-rate is 67% on templated prompts, but if you include freeform it drops to close to 29%. We also saw one bucket where hit-rate was 4%, which correlates to long tails where users append dynamic session ids.
01:12 Rachel Kim: Sorry can I interrupt — when you say templated prompts, are those our 40 canonical templates or the broader 120 set we talked about?
01:21 Marcus Chen: Good call. That 67% is for the curated 40 canonical templates that Novus flagged as stable. For the larger 120 set hit-rate is more like 45% after normalizing whitespace and removing session tokens.
01:35 Tom Alvarez: And that normalization was done in the middleware, right? Not at model entry?
01:41 Marcus Chen: Correct — we applied a light pre-tokenizer strip that removes UUID-like tokens and normalizes digits. But we didn't change template structure.
02:02 Priya Singh: Can you translate that into cost? Like what does 45% vs 67% mean for our monthly token bill?
02:10 Lena Ortega: We estimated — rough numbers — with current throughput the difference is about 18% in per-token compute. On our Dedicated cost model that maps to roughly $1.2k/month savings at your current volume when moving from 45% to 67% hit-rate. That’s just inference cost, excluding storage or infra.
02:38 Rachel Kim: That's helpful. What about latency impact? Any tail effects?
02:44 Marcus Chen: Yes: when KV hits we see average p95 drop from ~210ms to ~95ms on the request-path we profiled. Median moves from 120ms to 85ms. So it's meaningful for user experience.
03:05 Priya Patel: Quick note on measurement fidelity: we noticed some entries labeled as 'miss' that were actually partial hits — e.g., prefix matched but leftover tokens bypassed cache. We should change the logging to include 'partial_hit' classification.
03:27 Marcus Chen: Agreed. We can add a tri-state: full_hit / partial_hit / miss. That will help with tuning eviction policy.
03:40 Rachel Kim: Regarding eviction — what window are you using now?
03:43 Marcus Chen: Default is LRU with a 30-minute TTL for dynamic prompts and 6-hour sticky for canonical prompts. We can try bumping the canonical sticky to 24h for the pilot to see if that increases hit-rate without adverse mem pressure.
04:01 Tom Alvarez: Mem pressure on Dedicated nodes is a concern; we have constrained GPU RAM on the serving cluster. Any risk?
04:07 Marcus Chen: We'll simulate first. The runtime exposes a quantized footprint estimate per cached KV. If we see >75% memory utilization we'll fallback to eviction-first policy. Also, Redwood Optimize can recommend which entries to evict based on frequency.
04:26 Rachel Kim: Let's talk about prompt reuse. Our content team often adds subtle variations — salutations, time-of-day strings — which break fingerprints. How do we canonicalize without losing personalization?
04:40 Marcus Chen: Two approaches: 1) template canonicalization — enforce placeholders for variable fields (e.g., {user_name}, {order_id}), 2) fuzzy canonicalization — normalize non-critical tokens like greetings and dates before hashing. For your use-case I think a hybrid approach works: maintain personalization tokens but normalize greetings/dates.
05:05 Priya Singh: Who owns adding placeholders? Content team or Devs?
05:09 Rachel Kim: Content team owns templates but we'll need engineering support to implement placeholder extraction in the SDK.
05:18 Lena Ortega: Redwood can provide a small SDK patch that runs canonicalization heuristics on the client-side before sending to the runtime. It would be opt-in for the pilot.
05:30 Tom Alvarez: Would that change tokenization or just hashing key generation?
05:34 Marcus Chen: Just hashing/key generation — we don't modify the payload that the model sees, we keep original prompt body for inference. The cache key uses the canonicalized fingerprint only.
05:46 Rachel Kim: Ok makes sense.
05:50 Marcus Chen: Quick gotcha — when you canonicalize on client, you need consistent tokenizer across SDK and server. We recommend shipping a canonicalizer that mirrors the runtime tokenization.
06:04 Priya Patel: On the telemetry side, can you break hit-rate by user cohort? Mobile vs web?
06:09 Marcus Chen: Yup — we already have that. In your traffic mobile shows 12% higher reuse because mobile uses more canned flows. Web includes long-form search that is more freeform.
06:22 Rachel Kim: Great. For the experiments, can we run A/B where 50% of traffic uses SDK-canonicalizer and 50% baseline? We want to measure both hit-rate and any unintended regressions.
06:34 Lena Ortega: Absolutely. We can set up canary routing. We'll need the canonical prompt set first so we know the mapping.
06:42 Marcus Chen: On a separate note, we tried an early dedupe pass where we collapsed near-duplicate prompts via Levenshtein threshold 0.12 and saw hit-rate bump for templated flows from 67% to 73% but that introduced a few false merges for personalized marketing prompts. So we recommend a whitelist vs blacklist approach — only dedupe in flows you mark as safe.
07:08 Priya Singh: Can you show specific examples of the false merges?
07:12 Marcus Chen: Sure — I'll paste one in chat. Example A: 'Send discount code to {{user}} for cart abandonment' vs 'Send discount code to {{user}} for review request' — semantic difference but text similarity high so threshold triggered.
07:28 Rachel Kim: That's not acceptable for those flows. We can mark the marketing templates as no-dedupe.
07:34 Lena Ortega: Noted. We'll provide an annotation field you can set per-template.
07:40 Marcus Chen: On metrics capture — propose we add these to the weekly dashboard: full_hit_rate, partial_hit_rate, miss_rate, p50/p95 latency for hits vs misses, tokens_saved_estimate, and cost_delta_estimate.
07:59 Tom Alvarez: Sounds good.
08:04 Rachel Kim: Anything on security side? We need to ensure caching doesn't leak PII across tenants or users.
08:10 Lena Ortega: Important point. For this pilot we're isolating cache keys by tenant id and user-scoped keys for any prompts flagged sensitive. We also encrypt in-memory keys and have audit logs for cache access per request. Marcus, maybe call out the KMS integration?
08:25 Marcus Chen: We use the same KMS envelope for the runtime keys. Cache entries containing flagged sensitive tokens are stored in an encrypted bucket with HSM-managed keys. We'll include the relevant doc in follow-up.
08:36 Priya Singh: Can we add a privacy test — sample 1k hits and verify no cross-user keys?
08:41 Marcus Chen: Yes, run privacy sweep as part of the benchmark. We'll include that in the run plan.
08:50 Rachel Kim: Nice. Back to optimization — you mentioned tokenization differences. We saw small mismatches because the third-party tokenizer normalizes unicode differently. How do we keep deterministic fingerprints?
09:02 Marcus Chen: We recommend shipping Redwood's tokenizer shim in the SDK. That shim mirrors the runtime tokenization table and normalizes unicode, punctuation, whitespace.
09:12 Priya Patel: Implementation effort?
09:14 Marcus Chen: Minimal — it's a small JS/Python package. We'll provide it and can do a quick integration guide.
09:20 Rachel Kim: Ok. Let's recap the experiment matrix so we're aligned.
09:25 Lena Ortega: I'll summarize — Experiment A: client-side canonicalizer + SDK tokenizer for 50% traffic. Experiment B: bump canonical TTL to 24h for canonical templates only. Experiment C: dedupe with whitelist-only flows (marketing off). Benchmarks: measure full/partial/miss rates, p50/p95 latency, tokens_saved, cost_delta, and privacy sweep results.
09:54 Tom Alvarez: What timeline do you propose?
09:58 Marcus Chen: We can start staged rollout within 72 hours of receiving the canonical prompt CSV and your sign-off on TTL changes. So earliest bench run Friday if docs arrive Thursday.
10:12 Rachel Kim: We'll try to get the canonical set to you by end of day Thursday.
10:18 Priya Singh: One more ask — can Redwood provide an automated script that tags prompts with suggested placeholders using heuristics? That would speed content team's work.
10:28 Marcus Chen: We have a prototype; we'll include it in the share. It suggests placeholders and a confidence score. Human review still recommended.
10:38 Lena Ortega: Okay, last part — any blockers from legal/compliance or procurement?
10:44 Rachel Kim: Procurement is fine for the pilot. Legal asked for a short note about encryption-at-rest which Marcus will supply.
10:51 Marcus Chen: Will do.
10:54 Lena Ortega: Great, let's go through the action items.
10:57 Rachel Kim: Thanks everyone.
11:00 Meeting end.

Post-call notes: observed artifacts will be uploaded to the shared pilot folder: 'redwood/novus/pilot/cache-experiments'. Marcus to attach a sample log export (redacted) and the tokenizer shim repo link.
notes: Participants agreed to a three-experiment plan: A/B SDK canonicalizer, TTL extension, and whitelist-based dedupe. Privacy sweep and memory-pressure simulation required before 24h TTL change. Redwood to provide SDK shim, redact logs, and placeholder-suggestion prototype.
